# Launching eLife, Part 1

## Authors

- Randy Schekman †
- Mark Patterson
- Fiona Watt
- Detlef Weigel

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

The new open-access journal eLife has launched, making its first content available in PubMed Central. In addition to publishing science of the highest quality, the journal aims to improve both the peer-review process and the presentation of new research results.

claims.source_text: The new open-access journal eLife has launched
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a definitional statement about the journal's access model, representing established fact about the journal's characteristics at the time of publication

claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a factual statement about the operational status of the journal at the time of this manuscript

claims.claim: eLife has made its first content available in PubMed Central
claims.source_text: The new open-access journal eLife has launched, making its first content available in PubMed Central
claims.evidence_reasoning: This is a factual statement about a specific action taken by the journal regarding content distribution

results.result_reasoning: Claims C1-C3 represent verifiable factual statements about the journal's operational status and characteristics at the time of publication. The launch of eLife as an open-access journal and its content availability in PubMed Central are concrete, observable facts that can be independently confirmed and do not require experimental validation.

Claims C4-C6 represent stated aspirations and goals rather than demonstrated results. While these objectives are clearly articulated, the manuscript provides no evidence, methodology, or metrics to evaluate whether these aims will be or have been achieved. Assessment of these goals would require future evaluation of the journal's actual practices and outcomes.

Claims C7-C8 are implicit inferences about deficiencies in current scientific publishing practices. The manuscript provides no empirical evidence, literature review, or systematic analysis to support these assertions about the peer-review process or research presentation needing improvement. These claims rely entirely on unstated assumptions without supporting documentation.
